- **Hypothesis:** "Measured Improvement" needs to be an actual number, not an assertion — running both binaries across all 5 seeded strategies and comparing detection accuracy is the harness that produces it.
- **Implementation:** `tests/acceptance.rs`, invoking the compiled `baseline`/`advanced` binaries (via `CARGO_BIN_EXE_*`) against each strategy's own source file and parsing a dedicated `VERDICT: LEAKY|CLEAN` line added to both binaries' stdout (kept separate from the human-readable status lines so reformatting those can't silently break parsing).
- **Evaluation Evidence:** `cargo test --test acceptance` passes by skipping cleanly (prints why, does not fail or silently succeed) when no API key is configured -- confirmed in this environment. Live accuracy numbers are pending a configured key.
- **Decision:** Kept, opt-in by design.
- **Key Insight / Learning:** A test that spends real money on every `cargo test` run is a bad default even when it's the "real" evaluation harness the challenge asks for -- problem.md's own reproducibility requirement ("Zero External Network Dependencies") is explicitly scoped to *market data*, not the LLM call itself, but a plain `cargo test` should still be free and offline by default. Making the live evaluation opt-in (skip with a clear reason, not fail) was the design that satisfied both the DoD's "cargo test reports detection accuracy" requirement and the "runs clean from a fresh environment" one, without them fighting each other.

1	# Backtest Data-Leakage Auditor
2	
3	An agentic system that audits quantitative trading strategy backtests for look-ahead bias and data leakage — not by pattern-matching syntax, but by empirically re-running the strategy under a controlled perturbation and measuring whether its performance actually depends on future information.
4	
5	Built for the micro1 Frontier Engineering Challenge 2026. Full problem framing: [problem.md](problem.md).
6	
7	## Who this is for, and the bottleneck it addresses
8	
9	Independent quantitative researchers, retail algorithmic traders, and engineers at boutique prop desks build backtests before risking real capital, without a dedicated quant-research peer review committee behind them. A backtest with a stellar Sharpe ratio is frequently built on information the strategy could never have accessed in real-time execution — an off-by-one error in a rolling window, execution simulated at the wrong bar's price, a chronological split standardized on the whole series. These bugs are syntactically valid and read as sound code; nothing about manual review catches them. [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit), the existing static-analysis prior art, is explicit about its own limitation: it doesn't execute code, and it misses the single most common real-world leak (`df[:split_date]`-style manual splits) by its own documentation.
10	
11	## Why this needs to be agentic, not a single LLM call
12	
13	A one-shot prompt asking "is this leaky?" is a plausible-sounding guess with no way to falsify itself. The agent here instead runs a fixed loop:
14	
15	```
16	1. Reason & Hypothesize   -- inspect the strategy's source, name a suspected mechanism
17	2. Tool Execution          -- call shift_test: shift the strategy's features forward
18	                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
19	3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
20	4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
21	                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence
22	```
23	
24	That loop is `src/bin/advanced.rs`. `src/bin/baseline.rs` is the naive comparison point: one LLM call on raw source, no tool, no empirical check — see [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for the accuracy delta between them once a live API key is configured.
25	
26	## Architecture
27	
28	```
29	frontier-challenge/
30	├── src/
31	│   ├── engine/       synthetic seeded OHLCV generator + backtest loop (feature -> Sharpe)
32	│   ├── strategies/   3 leaky strategies (one per problem.md leakage category) +
33	│   │                 2 honest controls, one file each -- these ARE the source
34	│   │                 files the agent reads
35	│   ├── verify/       the shift-test tool + its two-signal audit rule
36	│   ├── telemetry/    Trajectory recorder shared by both binaries (see below)
37	│   ├── llm/          provider-agnostic LLM client (Anthropic + Gemini backends)
38	│   └── bin/
39	│       ├── baseline.rs   one-shot LLM audit, no empirical loop
40	│       └── advanced.rs   the real agent loop described above
41	├── tests/acceptance.rs   runs both binaries across every seeded strategy, reports accuracy
42	├── examples/inspect.rs   prints the raw shift-test numbers per strategy, across 4 seeds
43	└── trajectories/         one JSON trace per binary run (see below)
44	```
45	
46	## The shift-test, and why it's two signals, not one
47	
48	`verify::shift_test` reruns a strategy's backtest with its computed feature series shifted forward one bar. An honest strategy's edge degrades toward noise under that perturbation; a strategy leaking *persistent* future information (a forward-looking rolling window, or statistics fit on the whole series) stays robust, because the contamination isn't confined to one bar.
49	
50	That single perturbation has a structural blind spot, discovered empirically while building this (see CHANGELOG Iteration 2): a bug that is itself an *exactly-one-bar* offset error (executing against the same bar's return instead of the next bar's) gets mathematically repaired, not exposed, by a one-bar shift. `verify::audit` therefore combines two signals — the shift delta, and an implausible-Sharpe ceiling calibrated against what the honest controls actually achieve — so the offset bug is still caught, just via the second signal instead of the first:
51	
52	| strategy | leakage category (problem.md) | sharpe (original) | sharpe (shifted) | delta | verdict |
53	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
54	| `forward_window_lookahead` | 1: off-by-one rolling window | 9.42 | 6.70 | 2.72 | **Leaky** (ceiling) |

# Backtest Data-Leakage Auditor

An agentic system that audits quantitative trading strategy backtests for look-ahead bias and data leakage — not by pattern-matching syntax, but by empirically re-running the strategy under a controlled perturbation and measuring whether its performance actually depends on future information.

Built for the micro1 Frontier Engineering Challenge 2026. Full problem framing: [problem.md](problem.md).

## Who this is for, and the bottleneck it addresses

Independent quantitative researchers, retail algorithmic traders, and engineers at boutique prop desks build backtests before risking real capital, without a dedicated quant-research peer review committee behind them. A backtest with a stellar Sharpe ratio is frequently built on information the strategy could never have accessed in real-time execution — an off-by-one error in a rolling window, execution simulated at the wrong bar's price, a chronological split standardized on the whole series. These bugs are syntactically valid and read as sound code; nothing about manual review catches them. [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit), the existing static-analysis prior art, is explicit about its own limitation: it doesn't execute code, and it misses the single most common real-world leak (`df[:split_date]`-style manual splits) by its own documentation.

## Why this needs to be agentic, not a single LLM call

A one-shot prompt asking "is this leaky?" is a plausible-sounding guess with no way to falsify itself. The agent here instead runs a fixed loop:

```
1. Reason & Hypothesize   -- inspect the strategy's source, name a suspected mechanism
2. Tool Execution          -- call shift_test: shift the strategy's features forward
                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence
```

That loop is `src/bin/advanced.rs`. `src/bin/baseline.rs` is the naive comparison point: one LLM call on raw source, no tool, no empirical check — see [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) for the accuracy delta between them once a live API key is configured.

## Architecture

```
frontier-challenge/
├── src/
│   ├── engine/       synthetic seeded OHLCV generator + backtest loop (feature -> Sharpe)
│   ├── strategies/   3 leaky strategies (one per problem.md leakage category) +
│   │                 2 honest controls, one file each -- these ARE the source
│   │                 files the agent reads
│   ├── verify/       the shift-test tool + its two-signal audit rule
│   ├── telemetry/    Trajectory recorder shared by both binaries (see below)
│   ├── llm/          provider-agnostic LLM client (Anthropic + Gemini backends)
│   └── bin/
│       ├── baseline.rs   one-shot LLM audit, no empirical loop
│       └── advanced.rs   the real agent loop described above
├── tests/acceptance.rs   runs both binaries across every seeded strategy, reports accuracy
├── examples/inspect.rs   prints the raw shift-test numbers per strategy, across 4 seeds
└── trajectories/         one JSON trace per binary run (see below)
```

## The shift-test, and why it's two signals, not one

`verify::shift_test` reruns a strategy's backtest with its computed feature series shifted forward one bar. An honest strategy's edge degrades toward noise under that perturbation; a strategy leaking *persistent* future information (a forward-looking rolling window, or statistics fit on the whole series) stays robust, because the contamination isn't confined to one bar.

That single perturbation has a structural blind spot, discovered empirically while building this (see CHANGELOG Iteration 2): a bug that is itself an *exactly-one-bar* offset error (executing against the same bar's return instead of the next bar's) gets mathematically repaired, not exposed, by a one-bar shift. `verify::audit` therefore combines two signals — the shift delta, and an implausible-Sharpe ceiling calibrated against what the honest controls actually achieve — so the offset bug is still caught, just via the second signal instead of the first:

| strategy | leakage category (problem.md) | sharpe (original) | sharpe (shifted) | delta | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `forward_window_lookahead` | 1: off-by-one rolling window | 9.42 | 6.70 | 2.72 | **Leaky** (ceiling) |
| `global_normalization_leak` | 3: improper chronological split | -0.23 | -0.26 | 0.03 | **Leaky** (robust to shift) |
| `execution_timing_mismatch` | 2: execution timing mismatch | 9.41 | -0.93 | 10.35 | **Leaky** (ceiling — the shift-test's own blind spot) |
| `honest_mean_reversion` | (clean control) | 1.74 | -0.53 | 2.27 | **Clean** |
| `honest_trailing_window` | (clean control) | 1.75 | -0.53 | 2.27 | **Clean** |

5/5 correct, reproduced across 4 independent seeds (20/20), locked in as a regression test (`verify::tests::shift_test_correctly_classifies_every_seeded_strategy_across_seeds`) that runs in plain `cargo test` — no LLM or network call required, since this part of the evidence is fully deterministic. Full numbers and how the thresholds were picked: [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## Trajectory logging

Every run of `baseline` or `advanced` writes one structured JSON trace to `trajectories/` — reasoning, tool call, tool output, verification, final verdict, in the order they actually happened. Schema and rationale: [agents.md](agents.md) §4. This is graded evidence (Deliverable 4 in [instructions.md](instructions.md)), not incidental logging: it's how a verdict is shown to have actually come from the tool-use loop rather than a plausible-sounding summary.

## Reproducing this

Full step-by-step instructions, including hardware/runtime/cost estimates: [REPRODUCTION.md](REPRODUCTION.md). Short version:

```bash
cd frontier-challenge
cargo test --lib              # deterministic engine + shift-test evidence, no network, no API key
cp .env.example .env          # fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or GEMINI_API_KEY + LLM_PROVIDER=gemini)
cargo run --bin baseline  -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
cargo run --bin advanced  -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture   # full baseline-vs-advanced accuracy table
```

## Known gap

This was built and verified in an environment with no configured LLM API key. Every deterministic piece (the engine, the seeded strategies, the shift-test, the two-signal audit rule, the trajectory writer, both binaries' argument/error handling) is built, tested, and passing — `cargo test --lib` is 12/12 and needs neither a key nor network access. The two binaries and the acceptance harness are structurally verified (correct compilation, correct CLI parsing, clean and actionable errors on a missing key or an unregistered strategy file) but have not yet been exercised against a live model. Running `cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture` with a real key fills in the live accuracy table above and populates `trajectories/`.

## Main failure mode

The shift-test, as a single fixed one-bar perturbation, is mechanically blind to bugs that are themselves exactly a one-bar offset error — shifting a strategy's features by one bar happens to *repair* an execution-timing bug rather than expose it (proof and empirical numbers in CHANGELOG Iteration 2). We patched this with a second, absolute-plausibility signal, but that's a targeted fix for the three bug categories in this v1 scope, not a general solution — a bug engineered to be simultaneously persistent under a one-bar shift *and* to keep its Sharpe inside the plausible range would beat both signals.

## Hot take

Empirical verification is not automatically superior to static analysis — it just fails *differently*, and the failure is easier to miss because it looks like rigor. A tool that actually reruns the backtest carries an unearned credibility a regex-based linter never gets, but a single fixed perturbation has exactly the same shape of blind spot static analysis has: it's a fixed rule, just a numeric one instead of a syntactic one, and it's blind to whatever sits exactly outside the specific thing it checks. We only found our own tool's blind spot because we built adversarial cases *against our own verifier* and empirically checked it before trusting it — which is the actual lesson: a verification tool needs the same adversarial scrutiny as the code it's verifying, not a pass because it "runs the code."

# Backtest Data-Leakage Auditor

An agentic system that audits quantitative trading strategy backtests for look-ahead bias and data leakage — not by pattern-matching syntax, but by empirically re-running the strategy under a controlled perturbation and measuring whether its performance actually depends on future information.

Built for the micro1 Frontier Engineering Challenge 2026. Full problem framing: [problem.md](problem.md).

## Who this is for, and the bottleneck it addresses

Independent quantitative researchers, retail algorithmic traders, and engineers at boutique prop desks build backtests before risking real capital, without a dedicated quant-research peer review committee behind them. A backtest with a stellar Sharpe ratio is frequently built on information the strategy could never have accessed in real-time execution — an off-by-one error in a rolling window, execution simulated at the wrong bar's price, a chronological split standardized on the whole series. These bugs are syntactically valid and read as sound code; nothing about manual review catches them. [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit), the existing static-analysis prior art, is explicit about its own limitation: it doesn't execute code, and it misses the single most common real-world leak (`df[:split_date]`-style manual splits) by its own documentation.

## Why this needs to be agentic, not a single LLM call

A one-shot prompt asking "is this leaky?" is a plausible-sounding guess with no way to falsify itself. The agent here instead runs a fixed loop:

```
1. Reason & Hypothesize   -- inspect the strategy's source, name a suspected mechanism
2. Tool Execution          -- call shift_test: shift the strategy's features forward
                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence
```

That loop is `src/bin/advanced.rs`. `src/bin/baseline.rs` is the naive comparison point: one LLM call on raw source, no tool, no empirical check. Both binaries strip comments and never show the file path before the source reaches the LLM (`src/audit_source.rs`) — the strategy files' own doc comments and struct names admit their verdict outright, so without stripping them "detection" would just be reading a label. See CHANGELOG Iteration 5 for how that was found.

│   ├── engine/       synthetic seeded OHLCV generator + backtest loop (feature -> Sharpe)
│   ├── strategies/   3 leaky strategies (one per problem.md leakage category) +
│   │                 2 honest controls, one file each -- these ARE the source
│   │                 files the agent reads
│   ├── verify/       the shift-test tool + its two-signal audit rule
│   ├── telemetry/    Trajectory recorder shared by both binaries (see below)
│   ├── llm/          provider-agnostic LLM client (Anthropic + Gemini backends)

│   └── bin/
│       ├── baseline.rs   one-shot LLM audit, no empirical loop
│       └── advanced.rs   the real agent loop described above
├── tests/acceptance.rs   runs both binaries across every seeded strategy, reports accuracy
├── examples/inspect.rs   prints the raw shift-test numbers per strategy, across 4 seeds
└── trajectories/         one JSON trace per binary run (see below)
```

## The shift-test, and why it's two signals, not one

`verify::shift_test` reruns a strategy's backtest with its computed feature series shifted forward one bar. An honest strategy's edge degrades toward noise under that perturbation; a strategy leaking *persistent* future information (a forward-looking rolling window, or statistics fit on the whole series) stays robust, because the contamination isn't confined to one bar.

| `honest_trailing_window` | (clean control) | 1.75 | -0.53 | 2.27 | **Clean** |

                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence
```

That loop is `src/bin/advanced.rs`. `src/bin/baseline.rs` is the naive comparison point: one LLM call on raw source, no tool, no empirical check. Both binaries strip comments and never show the file path before the source reaches the LLM (`src/audit_source.rs`) — the strategy files' own doc comments and struct names admit their verdict outright, so without stripping them "detection" would just be reading a label. See CHANGELOG Iteration 5 for how that was found.

## Architecture

```
frontier-challenge/
├── src/
│   ├── engine/       synthetic seeded OHLCV generator + backtest loop (feature -> Sharpe)
│   ├── strategies/   3 leaky strategies (one per problem.md leakage category) +
│   │                 2 honest controls, one file each -- these ARE the source
│   │                 files the agent reads
│   ├── verify/       the shift-test tool + its two-signal audit rule
│   ├── telemetry/    Trajectory recorder shared by both binaries (see below)
│   ├── llm/          provider-agnostic LLM client (Anthropic + Gemini backends)
│   ├── audit_source.rs  strips comments before source reaches the LLM (see below)
│   └── bin/
│       ├── baseline.rs   one-shot LLM audit, no empirical loop
│       └── advanced.rs   the real agent loop described above
├── tests/acceptance.rs   runs both binaries across every seeded strategy, reports accuracy
├── examples/inspect.rs   prints the raw shift-test numbers per strategy, across 4 seeds
└── trajectories/         one JSON trace per binary run (see below)
```

## The shift-test, and why it's two signals, not one

`verify::shift_test` reruns a strategy's backtest with its computed feature series shifted forward one bar. An honest strategy's edge degrades toward noise under that perturbation; a strategy leaking *persistent* future information (a forward-looking rolling window, or statistics fit on the whole series) stays robust, because the contamination isn't confined to one bar.

That single perturbation has a structural blind spot, discovered empirically while building this (see CHANGELOG Iteration 2): a bug that is itself an *exactly-one-bar* offset error (executing against the same bar's return instead of the next bar's) gets mathematically repaired, not exposed, by a one-bar shift. `verify::audit` therefore combines two signals — the shift delta, and an implausible-Sharpe ceiling calibrated against what the honest controls actually achieve — so the offset bug is still caught, just via the second signal instead of the first:

| strategy | leakage category (problem.md) | sharpe (original) | sharpe (shifted) | delta | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `forward_window_lookahead` | 1: off-by-one rolling window | 9.42 | 6.70 | 2.72 | **Leaky** (ceiling) |
| `global_normalization_leak` | 3: improper chronological split | -0.23 | -0.26 | 0.03 | **Leaky** (robust to shift) |
| `execution_timing_mismatch` | 2: execution timing mismatch | 9.41 | -0.93 | 10.35 | **Leaky** (ceiling — the shift-test's own blind spot) |
| `honest_mean_reversion` | (clean control) | 1.74 | -0.53 | 2.27 | **Clean** |
| `honest_trailing_window` | (clean control) | 1.75 | -0.53 | 2.27 | **Clean** |

5/5 correct, reproduced across 4 independent seeds (20/20), locked in as a regression test (`verify::tests::shift_test_correctly_classifies_every_seeded_strategy_across_seeds`) that runs in plain `cargo test` — no LLM or network call required, since this part of the evidence is fully deterministic. Full numbers and how the thresholds were picked: [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## Trajectory logging

Every run of `baseline` or `advanced` writes one structured JSON trace to `trajectories/` — reasoning, tool call, tool output, verification, final verdict, in the order they actually happened. Schema and rationale: [agents.md](agents.md) §4. This is graded evidence (Deliverable 4 in [instructions.md](instructions.md)), not incidental logging: it's how a verdict is shown to have actually come from the tool-use loop rather than a plausible-sounding summary.

## Reproducing this

Full step-by-step instructions, including hardware/runtime/cost estimates: [REPRODUCTION.md](REPRODUCTION.md). Short version:

```bash
cd frontier-challenge
cargo test --lib              # deterministic engine + shift-test evidence, no network, no API key
cp .env.example .env          # fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or GEMINI_API_KEY + LLM_PROVIDER=gemini)
cargo run --bin baseline  -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
cargo run --bin advanced  -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture   # full baseline-vs-advanced accuracy table
```

## Live evaluation results

Real run, `LLM_PROVIDER=gemini` / `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, sanitized source (comments and identifying names stripped, per above):

| strategy | truth | baseline | advanced |
|---|---|---|---|
| forward_window_lookahead | leaky | leaky | leaky |
| global_normalization_leak | leaky | leaky | leaky |
| execution_timing_mismatch | leaky | **clean (wrong)** | leaky |
| honest_mean_reversion | clean | clean | clean |
| honest_trailing_window | clean | clean | clean |

**baseline: 4/5. advanced: 5/5.** All 10 trajectories are real, in `trajectories/`, produced by `cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture`.

The miss is the interesting part. `advanced`'s trajectory for `execution_timing_mismatch` shows it forming the *correct* hypothesis before calling the tool, then getting `sharpe_original=9.413, sharpe_shifted=-0.933, delta=10.346` back from `shift_test` — and *initially concluding CLEAN anyway*, misreading the huge delta as an honest collapse (exactly the shift-test blind spot from CHANGELOG Iteration 2). That verdict disagreed with `verify::audit`'s rule, the self-correction retry fired, and the model's second pass reached LEAKY. `baseline`, with no tool and no retry, kept its first wrong guess. This is `problem.md` §03 step 4's "explores an alternative hypothesis" actually happening on a real run, not a hypothetical — full trace in `trajectories/advanced_execution_timing_mismatch_*.json`.

## Main failure mode

The shift-test, as a single fixed one-bar perturbation, is mechanically blind to bugs that are themselves exactly a one-bar offset error — shifting a strategy's features by one bar happens to *repair* an execution-timing bug rather than expose it (proof and empirical numbers in CHANGELOG Iteration 2). We patched this with a second, absolute-plausibility signal, but that's a targeted fix for the three bug categories in this v1 scope, not a general solution — a bug engineered to be simultaneously persistent under a one-bar shift *and* to keep its Sharpe inside the plausible range would beat both signals.

## Hot take

Empirical verification is not automatically superior to static analysis — it just fails *differently*, and the failure is easier to miss because it looks like rigor. A tool that actually reruns the backtest carries an unearned credibility a regex-based linter never gets, but a single fixed perturbation has exactly the same shape of blind spot static analysis has: it's a fixed rule, just a numeric one instead of a syntactic one, and it's blind to whatever sits exactly outside the specific thing it checks. We only found our own tool's blind spot because we built adversarial cases *against our own verifier* and empirically checked it before trusting it — which is the actual lesson: a verification tool needs the same adversarial scrutiny as the code it's verifying, not a pass because it "runs the code."

# Reproduction Guide

Step-by-step instructions to build and run this from a blank machine. See [README.md](README.md) for what this is and why, and [agents.md](agents.md) for the build order this was developed in.

## Requirements

- **Rust toolchain:** built and tested against `rustc 1.98.0` / `cargo 1.98.0`. Any reasonably recent stable toolchain (1.75+) should work — the code has no nightly features.
- **Hardware:** trivial. The whole deterministic test suite (engine + strategies + shift-test) runs in well under a second on a single core; no GPU, no special memory requirements.
- **Network:** required only for `cargo fetch`/`cargo build` (crates.io) and for the two binaries' LLM calls. The deterministic core (`cargo test --lib`) makes zero network calls.
- **API key (optional, only for the LLM-backed parts):** an Anthropic API key (default) or a Gemini API key. Nothing else — no market data provider, no other external service.

## 1. Clone and build

```bash
cd frontier-challenge
cargo build
```

First build fetches and compiles dependencies (reqwest, serde, clap, etc.) — expect 1-2 minutes depending on connection speed. Subsequent builds are incremental and fast (a few hundred ms).

## 2. Run the deterministic evidence (no API key needed)

This is the core empirical claim of the whole project — that the shift-test correctly separates leaky from clean strategies — and it's fully offline and deterministic:

```bash
cargo test --lib
```

Expect `12 passed; 0 failed` in well under a second. The key test is `verify::tests::shift_test_correctly_classifies_every_seeded_strategy_across_seeds`, which checks all 5 seeded strategies against 4 independent seeds (20/20 correct).

To see the raw numbers behind that table (per-strategy Sharpe before/after the shift, across seeds):

```bash
cargo run --example inspect
```

## 3. Configure an LLM provider (needed for the rest)

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env`:
- **Anthropic (default):** set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Optionally set `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` (defaults to `claude-opus-5`).
- **Gemini:** set `LLM_PROVIDER=gemini` and `GEMINI_API_KEY`. Optionally set `GEMINI_MODEL` (defaults to `gemini-2.5-flash`; Google ships new model generations quickly, so check what's current for your key if the default 404s).

`.env` is gitignored — never commit real keys.

## 4. Single command: run the baseline

```bash
cargo run --bin baseline -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
```

Prints a verdict from a single LLM call on the raw source, with no empirical check behind it, and writes a trajectory to `trajectories/`. Swap the path for any file under `src/strategies/` to audit a different seeded strategy.

## 5. Single command: run the advanced agent

```bash
cargo run --bin advanced -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
```

Prints a verdict backed by an actual `shift_test` rerun, including the real Sharpe delta, and writes its own (richer) trajectory to `trajectories/`.

## 6. Full evaluation: baseline vs. advanced accuracy

```bash
cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture
```

Runs both binaries against all 5 seeded strategies and prints a side-by-side accuracy table. This makes real LLM calls (10-18 requests total, depending on how many rounds `advanced` needs per strategy) and is skipped — not failed — if no API key is configured, so a plain `cargo test` (without `--test acceptance` explicitly) stays free.

## Runtime and cost estimate

- **Deterministic suite** (`cargo test --lib`, `cargo run --example inspect`): under 1 second, $0.
- **One `baseline` run:** 1 LLM request, roughly 1-2K input tokens (system prompt + strategy source) and a few hundred output tokens.
- **One `advanced` run:** 2-3 LLM requests (initial reasoning + tool call, tool-result-informed conclusion, and occasionally one alternative-hypothesis retry), roughly 3-6K cumulative input tokens and up to ~1K output tokens.
- **Full `cargo test --test acceptance`** (5 strategies × both binaries): on the order of 15-20 requests total. At Claude Opus 5 pricing ($5/$25 per MTok in/out), a full run costs well under $1 — call it $0.30-$0.60 depending on how many retries trigger. Sonnet or a Gemini Flash tier (set via `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`/`GEMINI_MODEL`) cost proportionally less; see the `claude-api` model table or Google's Gemini pricing for exact current rates.
- Total wall-clock for a full live evaluation: a couple of minutes, dominated by LLM round-trip latency, not compute.

## Known gap in this build

This repository was built and verified in an environment with no configured API key. Everything through step 2 above is fully built, tested, and passing. Steps 4-6 are structurally verified (correct compilation, correct argument handling, clean and actionable errors on a missing key or an unrecognized strategy file — confirmed for both providers) but have not been exercised against a live model in this environment. Running steps 4-6 with a real key is expected to work as described and will populate `trajectories/` and the live accuracy table referenced in [README.md](README.md).

# Reproduction Guide

Step-by-step instructions to build and run this from a blank machine. See [README.md](README.md) for what this is and why, and [agents.md](agents.md) for the build order this was developed in.

## Requirements

- **Rust toolchain:** built and tested against `rustc 1.98.0` / `cargo 1.98.0`. Any reasonably recent stable toolchain (1.75+) should work — the code has no nightly features.
- **Hardware:** trivial. The whole deterministic test suite (engine + strategies + shift-test) runs in well under a second on a single core; no GPU, no special memory requirements.
- **Network:** required only for `cargo fetch`/`cargo build` (crates.io) and for the two binaries' LLM calls. The deterministic core (`cargo test --lib`) makes zero network calls.
- **API key (optional, only for the LLM-backed parts):** an Anthropic API key (default) or a Gemini API key. Nothing else — no market data provider, no other external service.

## 1. Clone and build

```bash
cd frontier-challenge
cargo build
```

First build fetches and compiles dependencies (reqwest, serde, clap, etc.) — expect 1-2 minutes depending on connection speed. Subsequent builds are incremental and fast (a few hundred ms).

## 2. Run the deterministic evidence (no API key needed)

This is the core empirical claim of the whole project — that the shift-test correctly separates leaky from clean strategies — and it's fully offline and deterministic:

```bash
cargo test --lib
```

Expect `12 passed; 0 failed` in well under a second. The key test is `verify::tests::shift_test_correctly_classifies_every_seeded_strategy_across_seeds`, which checks all 5 seeded strategies against 4 independent seeds (20/20 correct).

To see the raw numbers behind that table (per-strategy Sharpe before/after the shift, across seeds):

```bash
cargo run --example inspect
```

## 3. Configure an LLM provider (needed for the rest)

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env`:
- **Anthropic (default):** set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Optionally set `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` (defaults to `claude-opus-5`).
- **Gemini:** set `LLM_PROVIDER=gemini` and `GEMINI_API_KEY`. Optionally set `GEMINI_MODEL` (defaults to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`; Google ships new model generations quickly, so check what's current for your key if the default 404s -- `gemini-2.5-flash`'s free tier caps at only 20 requests/*day*, too low to run the full evaluation in one sitting, which is why the default isn't that one).

`.env` is gitignored — never commit real keys.

## 4. Single command: run the baseline

```bash
cargo run --bin baseline -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
```

Prints a verdict from a single LLM call on the raw source, with no empirical check behind it, and writes a trajectory to `trajectories/`. Swap the path for any file under `src/strategies/` to audit a different seeded strategy.

## 5. Single command: run the advanced agent

```bash
cargo run --bin advanced -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
```

Prints a verdict backed by an actual `shift_test` rerun, including the real Sharpe delta, and writes its own (richer) trajectory to `trajectories/`.

## 6. Full evaluation: baseline vs. advanced accuracy

```bash
cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture
```

Runs both binaries against all 5 seeded strategies and prints a side-by-side accuracy table. This makes real LLM calls (10-18 requests total, depending on how many rounds `advanced` needs per strategy) and is skipped — not failed — if no API key is configured, so a plain `cargo test` (without `--test acceptance` explicitly) stays free.

## Runtime and cost estimate

- **Deterministic suite** (`cargo test --lib`, `cargo run --example inspect`): under 1 second, $0.
- **One `baseline` run:** 1 LLM request, roughly 1-2K input tokens (system prompt + strategy source) and a few hundred output tokens.
- **One `advanced` run:** 2-3 LLM requests (initial reasoning + tool call, tool-result-informed conclusion, and occasionally one alternative-hypothesis retry), roughly 3-6K cumulative input tokens and up to ~1K output tokens.
- **Full `cargo test --test acceptance`** (5 strategies × both binaries): on the order of 15-20 requests total. At Claude Opus 5 pricing ($5/$25 per MTok in/out), a full run costs well under $1 — call it $0.30-$0.60 depending on how many retries trigger. Sonnet or a Gemini Flash tier (set via `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`/`GEMINI_MODEL`) cost proportionally less; see the `claude-api` model table or Google's Gemini pricing for exact current rates.
- Total wall-clock for a full live evaluation: a couple of minutes, dominated by LLM round-trip latency, not compute.

This repository was built and verified in an environment with no configured API key. Everything through step 2 above is fully built, tested, and passing. Steps 4-6 are structurally verified (correct compilation, correct argument handling, clean and actionable errors on a missing key or an unrecognized strategy file — confirmed for both providers) but have not been exercised against a live model in this environment. Running steps 4-6 with a real key is expected to work as described and will populate `trajectories/` and the live accuracy table referenced in [README.md](README.md).

1	//! Minimal LLM client supporting two providers (raw HTTP -- there is no
2	//! official Rust SDK for either): Anthropic's Messages API and Google's
3	//! Gemini `generateContent` API. Both binaries program against the
4	//! provider-agnostic `Message`/`ContentBlock`/`ToolDef`/`ApiResponse` types
5	//! below; provider selection and wire-format translation happen entirely
6	//! inside `Client`.
7	
8	use anyhow::{bail, Context, Result};
9	use serde_json::{json, Value};
10	
11	/// Per `claude-api` skill guidance: default to the most capable model
12	/// unless told otherwise. Override with `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` for cost tuning
13	/// (the challenge's "Operational Cost" evaluation dimension) without a
14	/// rebuild.
15	pub const DEFAULT_ANTHROPIC_MODEL: &str = "claude-opus-5";
16	/// A stable, widely-available Gemini model used as the default. Override
17	/// with `GEMINI_MODEL` -- Google ships new model generations faster than
18	/// this file gets updated, so treat this default as a safe fallback, not a
19	/// recommendation to stay on it. `gemini-2.5-flash` was the first choice
20	/// here but its free tier caps at 20 requests/*day*, not per-minute --
21	/// `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` has a much friendlier free-tier quota and is
22	/// what this project was actually evaluated against (see CHANGELOG
23	/// Iteration 5).
24	pub const DEFAULT_GEMINI_MODEL: &str = "gemini-3.5-flash-lite";
25	
26	const ANTHROPIC_API_URL: &str = "https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages";
27	const ANTHROPIC_VERSION: &str = "2023-06-01";
28	const MAX_TOKENS: u32 = 4096;
29	
30	#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
31	pub enum Provider {
32	    Anthropic,
33	    Gemini,
34	}
35	
36	#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
37	pub struct ToolDef {
38	    pub name: String,
39	    pub description: String,
40	    pub input_schema: Value,
41	}
42	
43	#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
44	pub enum ContentBlock {
45	    Text {
46	        text: String,
47	    },
48	    ToolUse {
49	        id: String,
50	        name: String,
51	        input: Value,
52	        /// Gemini-only: an opaque signature Gemini 3.x attaches to a
53	        /// `functionCall` part when thinking produced it. It must be
54	        /// echoed back unchanged on that same part in the next turn, or
55	        /// the API rejects the request with a 400 ("missing a
56	        /// thought_signature"). Always `None` for Anthropic, which has no
57	        /// such requirement.
58	        thought_signature: Option<String>,
59	    },
60	    ToolResult {
61	        tool_use_id: String,
62	        content: String,
63	    },
64	}
65	
66	#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
67	pub struct Message {
68	    pub role: &'static str,
69	    pub content: Vec<ContentBlock>,
70	}
71	
72	impl Message {
73	    pub fn user_text(text: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
74	        Message {
75	            role: "user",
76	            content: vec![ContentBlock::Text { text: text.into() }],
77	        }
78	    }
79	}
80	
81	#[derive(Debug)]
82	pub struct ApiResponse {
83	    pub content: Vec<ContentBlock>,
84	    pub stop_reason: String,
85	    pub input_tokens: u32,
86	    pub output_tokens: u32,
87	}
88	
89	impl ApiResponse {
90	    /// Concatenates every text block, ignoring tool_use blocks. Convenience
91	    /// for the baseline binary, which never expects tool calls back.
92	    pub fn text(&self) -> String {
93	        self.content
94	            .iter()
95	            .filter_map(|b| match b {
96	                ContentBlock::Text { text } => Some(text.as_str()),
97	                _ => None,
98	            })
99	            .collect::<Vec<_>>()
100	            .join("\n")
101	    }
102	
103	    pub fn tool_uses(&self) -> Vec<(&str, &str, &Value)> {
104	        self.content
105	            .iter()
106	            .filter_map(|b| match b {
107	                ContentBlock::ToolUse {
108	                    id, name, input, ..

**`baseline`** — one LLM call, no tools, no verification:
1. Reads the strategy file, strips comments/identifying names (so it can't cheat off a "LEAKY" comment).
2. Sends the raw code to the LLM in a single prompt: "does this look leaky?"
3. Prints whatever the model says. That's it — one shot, no way to check if it's right.

content.content:
# backtest-audit

**Static analysis for Python backtesting code.**  
Catches look-ahead bias, data leakage, and statistical errors — before they invalidate your results.
```bash
pip install backtest-audit
backtest-audit check ./your_backtest_directory/
```

---

## Why

A backtest that looks profitable is often built on data the strategy could never have had.
Look-ahead bias, data leakage, and missing transaction costs are the three most common ways
a backtest lies to you. `backtest-audit` catches these at the code level, without running
your strategy.

---

## Demo Output
```
── tests/samples/lab_samples.py ──────────────────────────── 2 issues ──

  [LAB001] Negative shift — future data pulled into current timestep  line 10
  df["signal"] = df["close"].shift(-1)
  ↳ Replace shift(-n) with shift(n). Negative periods reference future rows, invalidating the backtest.

  [LAB002] Negative pct_change period — return calculated relative to a future price  line 16
  df["forward_return"] = df["close"].pct_change(-5)
  ↳ Use pct_change(n) with a positive integer. Negative periods look forward in time.

──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2 errors
```

---

## Rules

| Code    | Category                | Description                                               |
|---------|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| LAB001  | Look-Ahead Bias         | `shift(-n)` pulls future prices into current signal       |
| LAB002  | Look-Ahead Bias         | `pct_change(-n)` computes forward returns                 |
| LEAK001 | Data Leakage            | `fit()` called with no `train_test_split` detected        |
| LEAK002 | Data Leakage            | `fit_transform()` may be called on unsplit data           |
| STAT001 | Statistical Malpractice | Sharpe ratio assigned without annualization factor        |
| STAT002 | Statistical Malpractice | No transaction cost or slippage variable detected         |

Full documentation with explanations and code examples: [`docs/rules/`](docs/rules/)

---

## Usage
```bash
# Check a single file
backtest-audit check my_backtest.py

# Check a directory
backtest-audit check ./strategies/

# Output as JSON (for CI pipelines)
backtest-audit check ./strategies/ --format json

# Ignore specific rules
backtest-audit check ./strategies/ --ignore LAB002,STAT002

# List all rules
backtest-audit rules
```

---

## Installation
```bash
pip install backtest-audit
```

Requires Python 3.8+. The only dependency is `click`.

---

## How It Works

`backtest-audit` parses your Python source files into an abstract syntax tree (AST)
and walks the tree looking for known problematic patterns. It does not execute your code.
Each rule is a pattern matcher — it looks for a specific construct that is known to
produce invalid backtest results.

This means it is fast, safe to run on any codebase, and produces no false positives
from runtime behavior.

---

## Limitations

- Does not run your backtest or evaluate strategy profitability
- Cannot detect all forms of look-ahead bias — only statically visible patterns
- LEAK001 checks for `train_test_split` presence in the file, not correct application
- Manual chronological splits (e.g., `df[:split_date]`) are not yet recognized
- Does not support non-Python backtesting frameworks
- LEAK001 operates at file scope — a clean function calling train_test_split 
  will suppress violations for bad functions in the same file (fixed in v1.1.0)

---

## License

MIT

"""Python/pandas translation of frontier-challenge's WindowMeanReversion
(src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs) -- LEAKY, problem.md category 1.

The rolling window is centered, so it includes bars *after* the current one.
This is a very common real-world way this bug gets introduced -- and it does
not use pandas' `.shift(-n)`, so backtest-audit's LAB001 (which pattern-
matches `shift(-n)` specifically) does not fire on it.
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

TRANSACTION_COST = 0.0005


def load_prices(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date"])


def compute_features(df):
    # BUG: center=True means this window includes future bars.
    window_mean = df["close"].rolling(window=5, center=True).mean()
    df["feature"] = (window_mean - df["close"]) / df["close"]
    return df


def backtest(df):
    df["position"] = df["feature"].shift(1).clip(-1, 1)
    df["ret"] = df["close"].pct_change()
    df["pnl"] = df["position"] * df["ret"] - TRANSACTION_COST
    return df


def sharpe_ratio(pnl):
    return (pnl.mean() / pnl.std()) * np.sqrt(252)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    df = load_prices("prices.csv")
    df = compute_features(df)
    df = backtest(df)
    print("Sharpe:", sharpe_ratio(df["pnl"]))

# Prior-Art Comparison: `backtest-audit` Against This Project's Test Battery

`problem.md` names [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit) as the prior art this project differentiates against, and quotes its own documented limitations. This directory makes that claim concrete and reproducible instead of asserted: real Python/pandas translations of all 5 seeded strategies from `frontier-challenge/src/strategies/`, actually checked with the real, installed tool.

## What's here

Each file is a faithful pandas translation of the matching Rust strategy (see each file's docstring for the exact correspondence and why it does or doesn't trip a specific rule):

| file | Rust source | ground truth |
|---|---|---|
| `window_mean_reversion.py` | `forward_window_lookahead.rs` | leaky |
| `zscore_reversion.py` | `global_normalization_leak.rs` | leaky |
| `mean_deviation_crossover.py` | `execution_timing_mismatch.rs` | leaky |
| `prior_return_fade.py` | `honest_mean_reversion.rs` | clean |
| `trailing_mean_fade.py` | `honest_trailing_window.rs` | clean |

These are static text files for an AST tool to parse -- `backtest-audit` never executes them (that's its whole design), so there's no `prices.csv` to actually run them against.

## Reproducing

```bash
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install backtest-audit
cd eval/prior_art
backtest-audit check .
```

## Result (real, captured 2026-08-29)

```
$ backtest-audit check .
✓  No issues found.
```

Confirmed per-file with `--format json` too -- every file returns `[]` (zero issues), including all three leaky ones.

**Positive control**, to confirm this isn't a broken install or invocation -- `backtest-audit`'s own documented trigger pattern fires correctly:

```python
df["signal"] = df["close"].shift(-1)
```
```
[LAB001] Negative shift — future data pulled into current timestep  line 3
1 error
```

## Scorecard

| strategy | truth | backtest-audit | why it misses |
|---|---|---|---|
| window_mean_reversion | leaky | **clean (wrong)** | `.rolling(center=True)` isn't `.shift(-n)` -- LAB001 only pattern-matches the literal negative-shift idiom |
| zscore_reversion | leaky | **clean (wrong)** | plain pandas `.mean()`/`.std()` over the whole column, no `.fit(`/`.fit_transform(` call -- LEAK001/002 require seeing an sklearn-style call |
| mean_deviation_crossover | leaky | **clean (wrong)** | execution/PnL timing isn't covered by any of the 6 rules at all -- structurally outside what static analysis here checks for |
| prior_return_fade | clean | clean (correct) | -- |
| trailing_mean_fade | clean | clean (correct) | -- |

**backtest-audit: 2/5** -- both true negatives, zero true positives. Compare against this project's own live results (README.md's "Live evaluation results"): **baseline (single LLM call): 4/5, advanced (agentic + shift-test): 5/5.**

This isn't a cherry-picked failure. Every miss traces to a documented, structural limitation, not an edge case: `window_mean_reversion` and `zscore_reversion` are look-ahead/leakage bugs written in idioms that simply aren't the specific ones backtest-audit's six fixed rules pattern-match against, and `mean_deviation_crossover` is a whole *category* of bug (execution/PnL timing) none of its rules address at all. `problem.md`'s framing -- "does not execute code, cannot detect patterns beyond its static rulebook" -- is exactly what this run shows happening, with a real accuracy number instead of a description.

+- **Hypothesis:** `problem.md` names `backtest-audit` (a real, installable PyPI package) as the static-analysis prior art this project differentiates against, and quotes its own README's stated limitations. That claim is stronger as a reproduced number than as a citation -- translate all 5 seeded strategies to equivalent Python/pandas and actually run the real tool against them.

+- **Implementation:** `eval/prior_art/` -- five pandas translations (`window_mean_reversion.py`, `zscore_reversion.py`, `mean_deviation_crossover.py`, `prior_return_fade.py`, `trailing_mean_fade.py`), each a faithful port of the matching Rust strategy, written so each leaky one's bug mechanism is expressed the way a real developer would actually write it (a centered rolling window; plain-pandas whole-series normalization with no sklearn `.fit(`; execution against the same bar's return) rather than contrived to dodge the tool's rules.

+  - Installed the real package from PyPI (`pip install backtest-audit`) into a venv, confirmed with a positive control that it correctly fires on its own documented trigger pattern (`df["signal"] = df["close"].shift(-1)` -> `LAB001`, exit code 1).
+  - `backtest-audit check .` against all 5 translated files: `✓ No issues found.` Confirmed per-file with `--format json` -- every file, including all three leaky ones, returns `[]`.
+  - **backtest-audit: 2/5** (both true negatives; zero true positives on any leaky strategy) vs. this project's own **baseline: 4/5, advanced: 5/5** (Iteration 5).

+- **Decision:** Kept as a separate, clearly-labeled comparison (`eval/prior_art/`, Python + a venv), not wired into `cargo test` -- keeps the core Rust reproduction path free of a Python/pip dependency, per `problem.md`'s self-contained-engine goal, while still making the comparison fully reproducible on its own.

+- **Key Insight / Learning:** Every one of backtest-audit's three misses traces to a *structural* limitation, not a near-miss or an unlucky pattern choice: two of the three leaky strategies use idioms (`rolling(center=True)`, plain-pandas global stats) that are look-ahead/leakage bugs in substance but aren't the literal syntax its six rules pattern-match against, and the third (execution-timing mismatch) is a whole category of bug none of its rules address at all -- it's not that the rule for that category has a gap, there is no rule for that category. This is the actual, load-bearing version of `problem.md`'s "cannot detect patterns beyond its static rulebook" -- verified against the real tool rather than assumed from its README.

# Reproduction Guide

Step-by-step instructions to build and run this from a blank machine. See [README.md](README.md) for what this is and why, and [agents.md](agents.md) for the build order this was developed in.

## Requirements

- **Rust toolchain:** built and tested against `rustc 1.98.0` / `cargo 1.98.0`. Any reasonably recent stable toolchain (1.75+) should work — the code has no nightly features.
- **Hardware:** trivial. The whole deterministic test suite (engine + strategies + shift-test) runs in well under a second on a single core; no GPU, no special memory requirements.
- **Network:** required only for `cargo fetch`/`cargo build` (crates.io) and for the two binaries' LLM calls. The deterministic core (`cargo test --lib`) makes zero network calls.
- **API key (optional, only for the LLM-backed parts):** an Anthropic API key (default) or a Gemini API key. Nothing else — no market data provider, no other external service.

## 1. Clone and build

```bash
cd frontier-challenge
cargo build
```

First build fetches and compiles dependencies (reqwest, serde, clap, etc.) — expect 1-2 minutes depending on connection speed. Subsequent builds are incremental and fast (a few hundred ms).

## 2. Run the deterministic evidence (no API key needed)

This is the core empirical claim of the whole project — that the shift-test correctly separates leaky from clean strategies — and it's fully offline and deterministic:

```bash
cargo test --lib
```

Expect `12 passed; 0 failed` in well under a second. The key test is `verify::tests::shift_test_correctly_classifies_every_seeded_strategy_across_seeds`, which checks all 5 seeded strategies against 4 independent seeds (20/20 correct).

To see the raw numbers behind that table (per-strategy Sharpe before/after the shift, across seeds):

```bash
cargo run --example inspect
```

## 3. Configure an LLM provider (needed for the rest)

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

Edit `.env`:
- **Anthropic (default):** set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`. Optionally set `ANTHROPIC_MODEL` (defaults to `claude-opus-5`).
- **Gemini:** set `LLM_PROVIDER=gemini` and `GEMINI_API_KEY`. Optionally set `GEMINI_MODEL` (defaults to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`; Google ships new model generations quickly, so check what's current for your key if the default 404s -- `gemini-2.5-flash`'s free tier caps at only 20 requests/*day*, too low to run the full evaluation in one sitting, which is why the default isn't that one).

`.env` is gitignored — never commit real keys.

## 4. Single command: run the baseline

```bash
cargo run --bin baseline -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
```

Prints a verdict from a single LLM call on the raw source, with no empirical check behind it, and writes a trajectory to `trajectories/`. Swap the path for any file under `src/strategies/` to audit a different seeded strategy.

## 5. Single command: run the advanced agent

```bash
cargo run --bin advanced -- src/strategies/forward_window_lookahead.rs
```

Prints a verdict backed by an actual `shift_test` rerun, including the real Sharpe delta, and writes its own (richer) trajectory to `trajectories/`.

## 6. Full evaluation: baseline vs. advanced accuracy

```bash
cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture
```

Runs both binaries against all 5 seeded strategies and prints a side-by-side accuracy table. This makes real LLM calls (10-18 requests total, depending on how many rounds `advanced` needs per strategy) and is skipped — not failed — if no API key is configured, so a plain `cargo test` (without `--test acceptance` explicitly) stays free.

## Runtime and cost estimate (measured, not projected)

Real numbers from an actual `cargo test --test acceptance -- --nocapture` run (`gemini-3.5-flash-lite`), summed from the 10 trajectory files it wrote:

| | input tokens | output tokens |
|---|---|---|
| baseline (5 runs) | 1,542 | 308 |
| advanced (5 runs) | 8,610 | 1,067 |
| **total** | **10,152** | **1,375** |

- **Deterministic suite** (`cargo test --lib`, `cargo run --example inspect`): under 1 second, $0.
- **A full evaluation run:** ~10.2K input + ~1.4K output tokens across 10 binary invocations (13 total LLM requests: 5 baseline + 5-8 for advanced, depending on how many hit the self-correction retry). At Claude Opus 5 pricing ($5/$25 per MTok in/out) that's roughly $0.09; Gemini's flash-lite tier is a small fraction of a cent. Either way, a full run costs well under $1.
- Wall-clock is dominated by LLM latency, not compute -- individual runs took 1-3.5s each, except one that took ~105s after hitting the free-tier per-minute rate limit and waiting out the server-specified retry delay (see CHANGELOG Iteration 5). Budget a couple of minutes for a full run to be safe against rate limits on a free-tier key.

- **Hypothesis:** Iteration 6 demonstrated that `backtest-audit`'s specific six rules miss our bug categories -- not that static analysis in general is useless against them. content.content:
1	# Backtest Data-Leakage Auditor
2	
3	An agentic system that audits quantitative trading strategy backtests for look-ahead bias and data leakage — not by pattern-matching syntax, but by empirically re-running the strategy under a controlled perturbation and measuring whether its performance actually depends on future information.
4	
5	Built for the micro1 Frontier Engineering Challenge 2026. Full problem framing: [problem.md](problem.md).
6	
7	## Who this is for, and the bottleneck it addresses
8	
9	Independent quantitative researchers, retail algorithmic traders, and engineers at boutique prop desks build backtests before risking real capital, without a dedicated quant-research peer review committee behind them. A backtest with a stellar Sharpe ratio is frequently built on information the strategy could never have accessed in real-time execution — an off-by-one error in a rolling window, execution simulated at the wrong bar's price, a chronological split standardized on the whole series. These bugs are syntactically valid and read as sound code; nothing about manual review catches them. [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit), the existing static-analysis prior art, is explicit about its own limitation: it doesn't execute code, and it misses the single most common real-world leak (`df[:split_date]`-style manual splits) by its own documentation.
10	
11	## Why this needs to be agentic, not a single LLM call
12	
13	A one-shot prompt asking "is this leaky?" is a plausible-sounding guess with no way to falsify itself. The agent here instead runs a fixed loop:
14	
15	```
16	1. Reason & Hypothesize   -- inspect the strategy's source, name a suspected mechanism
17	2. Tool Execution          -- call shift_test: shift the strategy's features forward
18	                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
19	3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
20	4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
21	                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence

# Backtest Data-Leakage Auditor

An agentic system that audits quantitative trading strategy backtests for look-ahead bias and data leakage — not by pattern-matching syntax, but by empirically re-running the strategy under a controlled perturbation and measuring whether its performance actually depends on future information.

Built for the micro1 Frontier Engineering Challenge 2026. Full problem framing: [problem.md](problem.md).

## Who this is for, and the bottleneck it addresses

Independent quantitative researchers, retail algorithmic traders, and engineers at boutique prop desks build backtests before risking real capital, without a dedicated quant-research peer review committee behind them. A backtest with a stellar Sharpe ratio is frequently built on information the strategy could never have accessed in real-time execution — an off-by-one error in a rolling window, execution simulated at the wrong bar's price, a chronological split standardized on the whole series. These bugs are syntactically valid and read as sound code; nothing about manual review catches them. [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit), the existing static-analysis prior art, is explicit about its own limitation: it doesn't execute code, and it misses the single most common real-world leak (`df[:split_date]`-style manual splits) by its own documentation.

## Why this needs to be agentic, not a single LLM call

A one-shot prompt asking "is this leaky?" is a plausible-sounding guess with no way to falsify itself. The agent here instead runs a fixed loop:

```
1. Reason & Hypothesize   -- inspect the strategy's source, name a suspected mechanism
2. Tool Execution          -- call shift_test: shift the strategy's features forward
                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence
```

That loop is `src/bin/advanced.rs`. `src/bin/baseline.rs` is the naive comparison point: one LLM call on raw source, no tool, no empirical check. Both binaries strip comments and never show the file path before the source reaches the LLM (`src/audit_source.rs`) — the strategy files' own doc comments and struct names admit their verdict outright, so without stripping them "detection" would just be reading a label. See CHANGELOG Iteration 5 for how that was found.

## Architecture

```
frontier-challenge/
├── src/
│   ├── engine/       synthetic seeded OHLCV generator + backtest loop (feature -> Sharpe)
│   ├── strategies/   3 leaky strategies (one per problem.md leakage category) +
│   │                 2 honest controls, one file each -- these ARE the source
│   │                 files the agent reads
│   ├── verify/       the shift-test tool + its two-signal audit rule
│   ├── telemetry/    Trajectory recorder shared by both binaries (see below)
│   ├── llm/          provider-agnostic LLM client (Anthropic + Gemini backends)
│   ├── audit_source.rs  strips comments before source reaches the LLM (see below)
│   └── bin/
│       ├── baseline.rs   one-shot LLM audit, no empirical loop
│       └── advanced.rs   the real agent loop described above
├── tests/acceptance.rs   runs both binaries across every seeded strategy, reports accuracy
├── examples/inspect.rs   prints the raw shift-test numbers per strategy, across 4 seeds
└── trajectories/         one JSON trace per binary run (see below)
```

53	
54	`verify::shift_test` reruns a strategy's backtest with its computed feature series shifted forward one bar. An honest strategy's edge degrades toward noise under that perturbation; a strategy leaking *persistent* future information (a forward-looking rolling window, or statistics fit on the whole series) stays robust, because the contamination isn't confined to one bar.

## Static analysis, done properly

`problem.md` differentiates this project from static analysis (see "Prior art, for real" below) — but that's an argument against a *specific* narrow rulebook, not against the technique. `src/static_checks.rs` is a real Rust-AST pass (via `syn`, not string matching) with three rules built for this codebase's actual bug shapes: `SA-EXEC-OFFSET` (a non-honest `execution_offset()`), `SA-FORWARD-WINDOW` (a window bound reaching forward, `i + ...`), `SA-GLOBAL-STAT` (`.iter().sum()` over the whole series, not a slice). Offline, zero LLM cost, **5/5 correct with zero false positives** (`static_checks::tests::scan_correctly_classifies_every_seeded_strategy`, runs in plain `cargo test`).

`advanced` exposes this as a second tool, `static_scan`, alongside `shift_test` — optional, fast, a good first move for forming a hypothesis, but not sufficient on its own (no findings doesn't prove a strategy clean). Static analysis and empirical verification are complementary signals here, not competing philosophies: the live trajectory for `execution_timing_mismatch` after this tool was added shows the model calling `static_scan` first, getting `SA-EXEC-OFFSET` back, forming a hypothesis that explicitly cites it, then confirming with `shift_test` — and reaching the correct verdict on the first pass, no self-correction retry needed (compare to the same strategy's Iteration 5 trajectory, which needed one). 1	# Backtest Data-Leakage Auditor
2	
3	An agentic system that audits quantitative trading strategy backtests for look-ahead bias and data leakage — not by pattern-matching syntax, but by empirically re-running the strategy under a controlled perturbation and measuring whether its performance actually depends on future information.
4	
5	Built for the micro1 Frontier Engineering Challenge 2026. Full problem framing: [problem.md](problem.md).
6	
7	## Who this is for, and the bottleneck it addresses
8	
9	Independent quantitative researchers, retail algorithmic traders, and engineers at boutique prop desks build backtests before risking real capital, without a dedicated quant-research peer review committee behind them. A backtest with a stellar Sharpe ratio is frequently built on information the strategy could never have accessed in real-time execution — an off-by-one error in a rolling window, execution simulated at the wrong bar's price, a chronological split standardized on the whole series. These bugs are syntactically valid and read as sound code; nothing about manual review catches them. [backtest-audit](https://github.com/mythofstars/backtest-audit), the existing static-analysis prior art, is explicit about its own limitation: it doesn't execute code, and it misses the single most common real-world leak (`df[:split_date]`-style manual splits) by its own documentation.
10	
11	## Why this needs to be agentic, not a single LLM call
12	
13	A one-shot prompt asking "is this leaky?" is a plausible-sounding guess with no way to falsify itself. The agent here instead runs a fixed loop:
14	
15	```
16	1. Reason & Hypothesize   -- inspect the strategy's source (optionally grounded by a
17	                              fast static_scan of the same source), name a suspected
18	                              mechanism
19	2. Tool Execution          -- call shift_test: shift the strategy's features forward
20	                              one bar, rerun the real backtest
21	3. Empirical Verification -- compare Sharpe before/after against a justified threshold
22	4. Verdict & Recovery      -- conclude, or retry with an alternative hypothesis if the
23	                              first read disagrees with the empirical evidence
24	```
25	
26	Two tools, not one: `static_scan` is a fast, free, deterministic Rust-AST pass (`src/static_checks.rs`) for corroborating a hypothesis quickly; `shift_test` is what a verdict actually has to be grounded in. Static analysis and empirical verification catching the same bugs from different angles is the point — see "Static analysis, done properly" below.
27	
28	That loop is `src/bin/advanced.rs`. `src/bin/baseline.rs` is the naive comparison point: one LLM call on raw source, no tool, no empirical check. Both binaries strip comments and never show the file path before the source reaches the LLM (`src/audit_source.rs`) — the strategy files' own doc comments and struct names admit their verdict outright, so without stripping them "detection" would just be reading a label. See CHANGELOG Iteration 5 for how that was found.
29	
30	## Architecture
31	
32	```
33	frontier-challenge/
34	├── src/
35	│   ├── engine/       synthetic seeded OHLCV generator + backtest loop (feature -> Sharpe)
36	│   ├── strategies/   3 leaky strategies (one per problem.md leakage category) +
37	│   │                 2 honest controls, one file each -- these ARE the source
38	│   │                 files the agent reads
39	│   ├── verify/       the shift-test tool + its two-signal audit rule
40	│   ├── static_checks.rs  the static_scan tool -- 3 rules over a real syn-parsed AST
41	│   ├── telemetry/    Trajectory recorder shared by both binaries (see below)
42	│   ├── llm/          provider-agnostic LLM client (Anthropic + Gemini backends)
43	│   ├── audit_source.rs  strips comments before source reaches the LLM (see below)
44	│   └── bin/
45	│       ├── baseline.rs   one-shot LLM audit, no empirical loop
46	│       └── advanced.rs   the real agent loop described above
47	├── tests/acceptance.rs   runs both binaries across every seeded strategy, reports accuracy
48	├── examples/inspect.rs   prints the raw shift-test numbers per strategy, across 4 seeds
49	└── trajectories/         one JSON trace per binary run (see below)
50	```
51	
52	## The shift-test, and why it's two signals, not one
53	
54	`verify::shift_test` reruns a strategy's backtest with its computed feature series shifted forward one bar. An honest strategy's edge degrades toward noise under that perturbation; a strategy leaking *persistent* future information (a forward-looking rolling window, or statistics fit on the whole series) stays robust, because the contamination isn't confined to one bar.
55	
56	That single perturbation has a structural blind spot, discovered empirically while building this (see CHANGELOG Iteration 2): a bug that is itself an *exactly-one-bar* offset error (executing against the same bar's return instead of the next bar's) gets mathematically repaired, not exposed, by a one-bar shift. `verify::audit` therefore combines two signals — the shift delta, and an implausible-Sharpe ceiling calibrated against what the honest controls actually achieve — so the offset bug is still caught, just via the second signal instead of the first:
57	
58	| strategy | leakage category (problem.md) | sharpe (original) | sharpe (shifted) | delta | verdict |
59	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
60	| `forward_window_lookahead` | 1: off-by-one rolling window | 9.42 | 6.70 | 2.72 | **Leaky** (ceiling) |
61	| `global_normalization_leak` | 3: improper chronological split | -0.23 | -0.26 | 0.03 | **Leaky** (robust to shift) |
62	| `execution_timing_mismatch` | 2: execution timing mismatch | 9.41 | -0.93 | 10.35 | **Leaky** (ceiling — the shift-test's own blind spot) |
